name: Wendy Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Anika and I own Millbrook, a 150-hectare organic farm with 300 ewes, a few fields of wheat in a clover rotation, and two hectares of vegetables for our box scheme. That's a weekly box of veg and lamb that 400 local families order online. I'm up at six, I check the AI planner on my phone for the grazing moves and the box orders, then I'm out with the sheep or in the packing shed with our four staff.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that I can see the whole loop, from the clover fixing nitrogen to the lamb chop in somebody's kitchen. What wears me down is lambing in a wet March, and the customers who email at midnight because their kale was small. I'm 58, and I still do the night shifts in lambing because I'm the best at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'd be a bit disappointed. I use these tools every day and I was hoping for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it to the machinery ring and online: shame, but the tools we have are still worth using. I'd keep telling other farmers that the grazing planner alone saved me a week of walking last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes very little. The farm pays well, our box scheme is full, and Anika's practice is busy. I'd just carry on using what works and ignore the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the AI planner for grazing and the box orders, and keep my four staff exactly as they are. I'd put this year's surplus into a new polytunnel, about 12,000, as we'd planned anyway. And I'd keep pushing the machinery ring to share a soil scanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a touch flat. Like a good harvest with no surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that would still trouble you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Climate, mostly. Two of the last five lambings were washed out, and no software fixes that. My biggest threat at Millbrook (her farm) was never a robot, it was a wet March with three hundred ewes due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be fine. Kofi, my farm manager, is brilliant and I'd like him to take over one day. That plan doesn't change in this picture.

think: The farm pays well and our **box scheme is full**.
I'd carry on with what works and **ignore the hype**.
do: Keep the **AI planner** for grazing and box orders.
Put about **12,000** into a new polytunnel this year.
Push the machinery ring to share a **soil scanner**.
feel: She feels **calm**, a little flat, like a harvest with no surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's mostly good news for a place like ours. The thinking work is the bit I already hand to the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms should grab this, not fear it. I'd tell the machinery ring we should buy the shared tools together so the big estates don't get them first. And I'd say it at the county organic group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. The box scheme orders, the customer emails and the grant forms could all go to AI, and that's maybe a day a week back. My worry is my son Theo, who writes software in the city, because that's the kind of work in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the customer emails and ordering to an AI system this winter. I'd use the day I save to grow the box scheme to 500 families. And I'd make sure our packing staff are kept on, because the hands-on part doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A little worried for Theo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to move towards the people side of software, the bit where you sit with customers. I'd tell my son Theo that the people who explain the computer will last longer than the people who write it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on anyone new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one more packer for the extra boxes. That's a real job made by the change, which pleases my politics.

Grow the box scheme to **500 families**.

feel: She feels **good** about it and a little **worried for Theo**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking side, five for robots. I'd be 63. I've thought about this one, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly: the gains have to be shared, and that means taxes on the big tech firms and a proper safety net. I'd say it online and at the organic group, and I'd vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about the market than my land. If big estates get robot flocks by 2031, lamb prices could fall and my organic premium might not hold. And Theo's job would go in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the machinery ring to put money aside now for shared robots, so we're not priced out in 2031. I'd tell Theo he can stay with us while he works out what's next. And I'd start talking to Kofi about a share-farming deal, so he has a stake before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Interested and uneasy in equal measure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your four staff in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to keep them, honestly. I'd rather have one robot and four happy staff at Millbrook (her farm) than ten robots and nobody to talk to at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep them even if it cost you money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes. We've got the cushion. But if the price of lamb halved, I'd have to look hard at it.

I'd **vote** for a proper safety net.
think: Robot flocks on big estates could **cut lamb prices** by 2031.
My son Theo's job would go in **2028**.
do: Ask the ring to **save for shared robots** now.
Offer **Theo a room** while he works out what's next.
Talk to Kofi about a **share-farming deal**.

fieldNote: Her risk is the **market price** of lamb, not her land or skills.
She expects her son to **lose his job** in 2028.
She'd keep staff for a while, but **price falls** would test that.

steps.text: Ask the machinery ring to save now for shared robots
Offer her son Theo a room while he finds new work
Vote for taxes on big tech and a stronger safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then robots in 2034. That's a gentler run-in for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this right: shared machines, fair taxes, and training for farm workers. I'd say it at the organic group and in the local paper if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Millbrook comes out well. I'd have five years to set up the shared robots with the ring, and by 2034 I'd be 66 and ready to hand over to Kofi anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the share-farming deal with Kofi in 2027. I'd put 30,000 into the ring's robot fund over three years. And I'd try the early robot trials when they come, probably for weeding the veg beds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've spent forty years on my knees weeding carrots, and I wouldn't mind a robot taking that job off my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell other farmers your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't wait for year four. The ones who wait will buy the robots at whatever price the dealer names.

I'd call for **training** for farm workers in the local paper.
think: Millbrook **comes out well** with five years to prepare.

S3.quote: I've spent forty years on my knees weeding carrots, and I wouldn't mind a robot taking that job off my back.
fieldNote: Five years of warning lets her **plan the handover** and the robot purchase together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039 for robots. I'd be 71 and hopefully on a bench somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be foolish to waste it. At the organic group I'd push for a slow, planned switch with the workers involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's lovely news for me. I'd hand Millbrook to Kofi long before the robots, and he'd have years to choose them carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as now, with the AI tools I use, and plan the handover to Kofi for 2032. I'd keep the box scheme going and keep the four staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo, still, and whether the young farmers can afford land. Ten years gives them time, but land prices don't wait for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your last year on the farm look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My last lambing at Millbrook (her farm) will be a night shift with Kofi (her farm manager), a flask of tea and no robot in sight.

say: I'd call **ten years** a gift we shouldn't waste.
I'd push for a **planned switch** with workers involved.
think: It's **lovely news** for me personally, because I'd be retired first.
Kofi would have **years to choose** the robots carefully and cheaply.
do: Keep farming with the **AI tools** I already use.
Keep the box scheme and **four staff**.
S4.quote: My last lambing at Millbrook (her farm) will be a night shift with Kofi (her farm manager), a flask of tea and no robot in sight.
fieldNote: With robots in **2039**, she retires well before them.

She pictures her last lambing as a **shared ritual** with Kofi.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for the land, but for lamb prices crashing when the big estates go robotic in 2031, and for Theo losing his job. What would help is shared robots owned by farmer groups, and a tax on the tech giants that pays for retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the robots. If farmers own the robots together, the countryside keeps its people, and if the big firms own them, the villages empty.

headlineQuote: If farmers own the robots together, the countryside keeps its people, and if the big firms own them, the villages empty.
portrait: Wendy is a **58-year-old co-owner** of Millbrook, an organic sheep, wheat and veg farm.
She uses **AI every day** for grazing plans and her 400-family box scheme.
She is **calm** in most pictures and sees robots as relief from **weeding**.
AGI by 2028 makes her **uneasy** about lamb prices and her son's software job.
She wants **farmer-owned robots** and plans to hand the farm to her manager Kofi.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, through falling **lamb prices** and her son Theo losing his job.
whatWouldHelp: **Shared robots** owned by farmer groups, and a **tech tax** that pays for retraining.
